strengths: Novel and well-motivated research direction: the paper presents the first large-scale (12.8M DataComp subset) study of 2D Gaussian Splatting as a substrate for contrastive vision–language alignment, a genuinely underexplored area relative to post-hoc token reduction methods (ToMe, PruMerge, VisionZip, etc.).

Substantial systems contribution: batched CUDA kernels, structured initialization, and L1/luminance-aware pruning enable 90× faster fitting and ~97% GPU utilization, making million-scale GS fitting feasible. The kernel design description (projection/rasterization tiling, inverted backward partitioning) is concrete enough to assess.

Honest reporting: the authors candidly state that GS encoders trail RGB baselines by 3–5 points, that training from scratch performs worse (Fig. 7), and that codec-side quantization is omitted. This transparency is commendable.

Reasonable architectural adaptation: the splat-aware stem (Fourier positional encoding, log-scaled covariances, gating, z-score normalization) plus Perceiver resampler with a mostly frozen RGB-pretrained backbone is a sensible parameter-efficient design, and the ablation over splat counts (400–3136) and output token counts (98 vs 196) shows thoughtful exploration.

The paper is generally well written, with clear motivation (edge–cloud transfer costs, token explosion) and a well-organized taxonomy of related work on token reduction and alternative image representations.
weaknesses: Missing the most important baseline for the paper's core claim: the motivating argument is transmission efficiency relative to compressed pixel formats, yet there is no comparison against simply transmitting JPEG (or similar) inputs through the same encoder. Without this, the central 'transmission-efficient substrate' claim is unsupported; the energy/bandwidth figures (Section 2) are never empirically connected to the proposed pipeline.

Absolute performance is weak and the framing overstates it: 13–15% top-1 zero-shot ImageNet-1K against an 18.5% RGB teacher is a ~25–30% relative gap, described as 'meaningful zero-shot performance.' The RGB baseline itself (38M model, 12.8M samples, 512 width) is modest, so the comparison surface is narrow.

The token-explosion motivation is only partially addressed: the representation uses up to 3,136 splats (more tokens than a ViT-B/16's 576 patches), and compression is measured in bytes (float16 splat parameters), not tokens. The reduction to 196/98 tokens via the Perceiver resampler is functionally similar to post-hoc token compression methods the paper positions itself against.

The 90× speedup conflates batching with algorithmic improvement: it is measured against a non-batched baseline codebase [37], so the fair algorithmic contribution is unclear. No end-to-end wall-clock comparison for the full dataset-fitting pipeline is provided.

Limited evaluation breadth: only ImageNet-1K zero-shot accuracy is reported; no retrieval, no VQA/multimodal benchmarks despite the token-reduction motivation, no error bars or multiple seeds, and single-node 8×H100 runs without compute-matched comparisons to RGB training.

Questionable design choices without ablation: luminance-based pruning assumes low-luminance regions carry minimal semantic information, which is not generally true (dark objects, night scenes); the pruning strategy's effect on downstream alignment quality is never quantified. The individual GS-stem components (Fourier encoding, gating, z-score normalization) are not ablated.

Several supporting results are thin: structured initialization and pruning are shown on essentially one image (Figs. 3–4) with PSNR on a single example; compression ratios are computed with unquantized float16 parameters, so the claimed 3–23.5× savings may not reflect a deployable codec.

The from-scratch results (Fig. 7) are relegated to a brief mention, yet they materially undermine the 'learnable substrate' narrative — the positive results depend entirely on distilling an RGB-pretrained backbone, leaving open whether 2DGS is truly viable as a native representation.

Reproducibility is limited: code is only promised ('will soon be open-sourced'), the DataComp subset selection process is not specified, and key hyperparameters for the 2DGS fitting stage (iterations, learning rates, splat budget selection per image) are incomplete.

strengths: Novel and interesting research direction: this appears to be the first systematic, large-scale study of 2D Gaussian Splatting as a substrate for contrastive vision–language alignment, moving beyond post-hoc token pruning.

Substantial systems contribution: batched CUDA kernels with structured initialization and L1-based pruning enable 2DGS fitting at scale (90× speedup, 97% GPU utilization), which is a prerequisite for the training experiments and could benefit the community.
Structured initialization is a sensible, well-motivated idea for the 2D image case, with quantified evidence (33.07 vs 21.09 PSNR at 4,900 Gaussians) and qualitative visualizations.

The paper is honest about its limitations: it explicitly states that GS encoders trail RGB baselines and that from-scratch training performs worse, and it includes ablations over splat counts (400–3136), token counts (98 vs 196), and compression ratios.
The adaptation recipe (frozen RGB-pretrained backbone + splat-aware stem + Perceiver Resampler, ~7% trainable parameters) is reasonable and clearly described.
weaknesses: The central claim that 2DGS is a 'viable multimodal substrate' is weakly supported and confounded. The best results come almost entirely from a frozen RGB-pretrained ViT backbone (Fig. 7 shows from-scratch GS training performs significantly worse), so the demonstrated semantic capability largely reflects RGB pretraining, not the Gaussian representation itself. The paper's positioning overstates what the evidence shows.

Critical missing baselines: (a) no comparison against simply transmitting JPEG-compressed or downscaled pixels through the same frozen backbone + adaptation stem — JPEG achieves comparable or better compression ratios than the reported 3–20× (computed with float16 splat parameters), so the claimed transmission-efficiency advantage is not established; (b) no comparison against other compact/alternative representations (INRs, VQ tokenizers) under the same protocol.

Absolute results are weak and the operating point is small: 13–15% top-1 zero-shot ImageNet-1K vs. an already modest RGB teacher at 18.5%, trained on only a 12.8M DataComp subset. At this scale, small differences are hard to interpret and the gap to realistic CLIP performance is enormous, limiting the strength of the 'viability' conclusion.

The end-to-end motivation is not evaluated: the paper motivates the work with edge–cloud energy/bandwidth arguments, but never measures energy, latency, or bandwidth of the full pipeline, and the cost of on-device 2DGS fitting (multiple seconds per image before optimization) is not accounted for.

The luminance-based pruning heuristic is under-justified: low-luminance regions can carry significant semantic content (dark objects, shadows, night scenes), and the pruning evaluation (Fig. 4) only measures reconstruction quality, not downstream zero-shot accuracy, so its impact on alignment is unknown.
Evaluation breadth is narrow: only zero-shot ImageNet-1K classification on one DataComp subset; no retrieval, no VQA or other multimodal benchmarks, and no variance/seeds reported.

Some inconsistencies and overclaiming: compression ratios are quoted variously as 3–20× (abstract, Fig. 6), 3–23.5× (Sec. 5.2), and 3–20× (conclusion); the 90× speedup compares a batched implementation against an unbatched baseline, which is partly apples-to-oranges; code is only promised ('will soon be open-sourced'), limiting reproducibility at review time.

Writing/positioning: Section 2's related-work framing ('are patch-based encoders truly the right substrate?') is asserted rather than demonstrated, and phrases like 'viable alternative visual encoding' and 'clear pathways for closing the remaining performance gap' are not substantiated by the presented experiments.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored question: whether 2D Gaussian Splatting can serve as a visual substrate for large-scale contrastive vision–language alignment. The related-work positioning is fair and clearly delineates this from prior small-scale efforts (GViT, GaussianToken).

The systems contribution is real and substantial: batch-aware CUDA kernels, structured initialization (grid positions, isotropic covariance, mean-color inheritance), and L1/luminance-based pruning enable fitting millions of splat-encoded images, with a well-documented 90x speedup and 97% GPU utilization measured with Nsight Compute (Fig. 2).

The experimental design is honest and self-critical: the paper openly reports that GS encoders trail the RGB teacher (13–15% vs. 18.5% top-1), includes a from-scratch training comparison showing it underperforms parameter-efficient adaptation (Fig. 7), and clearly states limitations in the conclusion.

The proposed GS stem (Fourier positional encoding, log-scaled covariances, gated sigmoid linear layer, z-score normalization, Perceiver Resampler) is a sensible, well-motivated design for handling variable-length, continuous Gaussian parameter sets, and training only ~7% of parameters is an efficient transfer recipe.

Results show sensible behavior: accuracy is stable across splat counts (400–3136) and compression ratios up to 12x, and the 196-token resampler outperforms the 98-token variant, supporting the claim that the architecture robustly consumes sparse splat representations.
weaknesses: The central scientific claim is not fully supported by the evidence. The motivating hypothesis is that splat representations preserve 'information critical for downstream learning while substantially reducing transmission overhead,' but the paper never runs the essential control: an encoder trained on JPEG-compressed or downsampled pixels at the same byte budget, or an RGB CLIP encoder fed with splat renderings. Without this, the 3–23.5x compression numbers cannot be interpreted—JPEG already achieves 10–50x compression, and it remains unknown whether splats offer any semantic advantage over simply transmitting compressed pixels.

Absolute performance is very weak: 13–15% top-1 zero-shot ImageNet-1K accuracy (30–35% top-5) is far below any competitive CLIP model, and even the RGB teacher at 18.5% top-1 suggests the base training setup itself is under-tuned relative to published DataComp results at the 12.8M scale. The 'meaningful zero-shot performance' framing overstates results that are only a few points above what the weak teacher provides.

Evaluation breadth is limited to a single benchmark (zero-shot ImageNet-1K) with no retrieval, no VQA, and no per-class or failure analysis. No error bars, seeds, or statistical significance are reported for any comparison, and key experimental details (fitting iterations, splat point selection per image, train/test consistency of splat budgets) are underspecified, limiting reproducibility—particularly since the code is only promised to be 'soon open-sourced.'

The edge–cloud energy motivation is asserted but never measured. The fitting process itself is compute-intensive (thousands of optimization iterations per image on the edge device), and the paper provides no accounting of end-to-end energy, latency, or bandwidth that would substantiate the transmission-efficiency argument; the cited energy statistics remain disconnected from the actual system.

Several algorithmic contributions are relatively standard or incremental: grid/mean-color initialization and L1-based sparsification are simple heuristics, and the luminance-based pruning rationale (low-luminance regions contain 'minimal visual information') is questionable—dark regions can be semantically important—yet no ablation isolates the contribution of pruning to downstream accuracy.

The 90x speedup is measured against a modified baseline ([37]) that, as described, lacks batch support; the comparison between a batched implementation and a per-image baseline conflates algorithmic contribution with an apples-to-oranges systems comparison, and no wall-clock end-to-end numbers (fitting time per image at production settings) are given.

The transfer-learning setup introduces a potential circularity concern that is not analyzed: the GS encoder adapts a frozen RGB teacher using splats fitted from the very same RGB images, and the paper does not analyze what information the splat bottleneck actually removes or preserves (e.g., via probing or representation similarity).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem framing: the paper is presented as the first large-scale exploration of 2D Gaussian Splatting as an input substrate for contrastive vision-language pretraining, moving beyond post-hoc token pruning, and this positioning is clearly articulated with relevant related work (GViT, GaussianToken, GaussianImage, INR-based approaches).

Genuine systems contribution: batched CUDA kernels for 2DGS fitting, with credible profiling evidence (Nsight Systems breakdown in Table 3, kernel/memory percentages, batch-size scaling), making offline fitting of 12.8M images feasible (~25-53 GPU-hours per configuration, Table 4).

Practical algorithmic improvements for 2DGS fitting itself: structured initialization (uniform grid positions, cell-fitted isotropic covariance, cell-average color) yields large PSNR gains over random init (35.25 vs 28.24 at 4900 points), and the L1 + luminance-threshold pruning sweep (Fig. 4, Fig. 8) is a careful, systematic study of compression/fidelity trade-offs.

Thorough experimental protocol: 38 zero-shot datasets from the CLIP benchmark, four Gaussian budgets crossed with two token counts, and unusually extensive appendix ablations (distillation strategy, distillation loss variants, stem architectures, normalization, point transformers, from-scratch training, rendered-pixel control experiment).

Honest self-assessment in the Discussion: the authors explicitly acknowledge that GS performance is upper-bounded by the RGB teacher, that from-scratch GS CLIP training converges poorly, that the pipeline operates on non-pruned FP16 splats, and identify GS-native architecture design as an open problem.
The 'rendering back into pixels' control experiment (Appendix 11.6) is a thoughtful diagnostic that isolates where the performance loss originates (lossy compression vs. the GS encoder itself).
weaknesses: The headline efficiency claim (3x-23.5x compression) is measured against uncompressed RGB, not against standard codecs. JPEG/WebP at 224x224 routinely achieves comparable or better compression with ubiquitous hardware decoding; a JPEG (or learned-codec) baseline at matched bitrates is a conspicuous omission, and without it the practical edge-cloud transmission argument is not substantiated. Fitting also imposes a large one-time preprocessing cost (~150 GPU-hours total plus a few seconds per batch at inference time for new images) that is never weighed against the transmission savings it is meant to enable.

The 90x speedup is measured against a non-batched baseline codebase (LIG/gsplat2d), so much of the gain likely reflects batching rather than algorithmic novelty; the fairer within-batch comparisons in Table 3 (e.g., 1.86x at batch 128) suggest the contribution is more incremental than the abstract implies.

The central 'viability of 2DGS as a substrate' claim is significantly circular: the two-stage recipe distills a frozen RGB teacher, so GS performance is upper-bounded by the RGB baseline by construction, and the rendered-pixel control shows the GS encoder extracts mostly what is recoverable from the compressed surrogate. This weakens the evidence that 2DGS is a fundamentally better representation rather than a lossy compressor coupled to a standard ViT.

Absolute performance is low and uneven: mean zero-shot accuracy of 22% (196 tokens), with catastrophic GS failures on distribution-shifted datasets (fer2013 drops from 17.4 to 7.2; diabetic retinopathy from 38.3 to ~3-5 relative accuracy 0.08-0.21), indicating fragility that the '90-98% of baseline' summary understates.

Scale and strength of the evidence are limited: a 12.8M-pair DataComp subset, a 38M-parameter width-512 ViT-B/16 (Small) teacher, and only zero-shot classification are evaluated; no retrieval, no VQA/downstream multimodal results, no comparison to alternative compact representations (INRs, VQ tokenizers) under identical training conditions.

Reproducibility is not yet established: the paper states the codebase 'will soon be open-sourced,' but no artifact is available at review time, and several pipeline details (e.g., exact distillation hyperparameters, per-configuration batch schedules) live only in brief appendix descriptions.

Some claimed advantages are asserted rather than demonstrated: e.g., token-count reduction of 196 to 98 gives <2% relative change for GS, but the finetuned 98-token RGB baseline in Table 7 (0.95 relative) nearly matches GS 98-token results, blurring the claimed token-efficiency advantage.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting and underexplored question: whether 2D Gaussian Splatting can serve as a visual substrate for vision–language pre-training, and it constitutes (to my knowledge) the first large-scale (12.8M DataComp) study of this kind.

Substantial engineering effort is evident: batched CUDA kernels for 2DGS fitting with profiling evidence (Nsight Systems results in Table 3), structured initialization with clear PSNR gains (35.25 vs 28.24 at 4900 points), and a well-executed pruning study (Figs. 4, 8).

The evaluation breadth is respectable: 38 zero-shot benchmarks, four Gaussian budgets, two token counts, and a large set of appendix ablations (distillation strategies, normalization, stem architectures, from-scratch training, rendered-RGB control experiments) that probe where the gains come from.

The discussion and appendix are unusually candid about limitations: the two-stage recipe is fundamentally upper-bounded by the RGB teacher, GS is more sensitive to distribution shift, and pruning is not yet integrated into the alignment pipeline.
weaknesses: The core efficiency narrative does not hold up under scrutiny. The edge–cloud motivation rests on transmission savings, but the 2DGS fitting must happen at the edge (or a gateway), and the paper itself reports that fitting 'still requires on the order of a few seconds per batch' even with the optimized kernels. This is vastly more expensive than JPEG encoding, undermining the claimed energy/bandwidth benefit; the ~157 total GPU-hours spent pre-fitting 12.8M images offline (Table 4) further weakens the 'efficiency' framing.

The method is distillation-bound rather than a demonstration of alignment from GS inputs. Since Stage 1 matches CLS embeddings of a frozen RGB teacher and Stage 2 fine-tunes a shared backbone, the result is essentially 'CLIP inputs can be lossily compressed with modest accuracy loss.' The most obvious competing baselines are missing: JPEG-encoded inputs fed to the same encoder, post-hoc token reduction methods (VisionZip, ToMe, cluster-based aggregation, all cited in Sec. 2), and the closely related GaussianToken and GViT, none of which are empirically compared.

The central claim that GS provides 'condensed semantic signal' is not well supported by the paper's own numbers. The RGB 98-token baseline with 5-epoch fine-tuning reaches 0.95 relative accuracy (Table 7) — essentially matching GS-3136 at 0.96 — using a trivial token-merging proxy, and the 196-token GS models (0.91–0.98) are never compared against RGB token-pruning at matched token counts.

Absolute performance is weak across the board (baseline mean 22.2%, GS variants 19.4–20.4%), and relative-accuracy claims of 90–98% are computed at this low operating point. Individual failures are severe (e.g., diabetic retinopathy collapses from 38.3% to 3–4%, a near-random-level result, for all GS variants), which the text acknowledges only briefly as distribution-shift sensitivity.

Headline numbers are presented inconsistently in the paper's favor: the 90× speedup is quoted for the 400-point configuration in Fig. 2, while the more representative 4000-point configuration in Table 3 shows 46.7×; and compression ratios use unquantized FP16 splats (the discussion concedes pruning was not applied in the alignment pipeline), so the reported 3–23.5× is a generous lower bound on cost rather than an achieved system benefit.

Because the paper is positioned as 'the first step toward a fundamentally different paradigm,' the burden of showing why 2DGS beats simpler compact representations is high; as written, the evidence mainly shows that a heavily engineered lossy compressor distills into CLIP without catastrophic degradation, which is an interesting negative/neutral result but not yet a convincing case for the new paradigm.

Reproducibility is currently limited: code is only promised ('will soon be open-sourced'), and several key details (exact distillation dataset handling, perceiver query initialization, text-adapter configuration) are spread across the appendix.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated research direction: the paper is the first large-scale exploration of 2D Gaussian Splatting as a visual substrate for contrastive vision-language pretraining, going beyond post-hoc token reduction toward an alternative representation-first paradigm.

Substantial systems contribution: batch-aware CUDA kernels with reported 90× fitting speedup over the [41] baseline, 97% GPU utilization, and detailed Nsight profiling (Table 3) that demonstrates the work needed to make 2DGS fitting feasible at 12.8M-image scale.

Structured initialization is a sensible, well-argued idea for the 2D setting (grid positions, cell-average color, isotropic covariance), with clear empirical gains (35.25 vs 28.24 PSNR at 4900 points; 22.04 vs 17.77 at 400 points) and supporting qualitative figures.

Unusually thorough empirical study for this scale: 38-dataset zero-shot evaluation, four Gaussian budgets × two token counts, and extensive appendix ablations (distillation vs. scratch training, distillation loss variants, stem architectures, normalization, logit-scale/learning-rate/text-freezing sensitivity, rendered-RGB surrogate experiments).

Candid and insightful discussion of limitations, including that GS performance is upper-bounded by the RGB teacher, sensitivity to distribution shift, the non-trivial fitting cost, and that pruning is not yet integrated into the alignment pipeline.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claim is not established against the relevant comparison point. Compression ratios (3×–23.5×) are computed only against raw uncompressed RGB; no comparison to JPEG/WebP/AVIF rate-distortion is provided, despite the paper's own acknowledgment that JPEG is the practical transmission format and that GaussianImage-style quantization achieves far more aggressive compression. Without a codec baseline, the edge–cloud transmission benefit remains speculative.

The energy/transmission motivation is not empirically validated: no measurements of actual bandwidth, latency, or energy savings in an edge–cloud setting are reported, and the fitting stage itself requires tens of GPU-hours (25–53 GPU-hrs per configuration for 12.8M images, Table 4) plus seconds-per-batch fitting — an assumption that edge devices can perform this preprocessing is unsupported.

The evaluation baseline is weak: a ViT-B/16 (Small) trained on only 12.8M DataComp pairs achieves ~22% average zero-shot accuracy, far below even moderate-scale CLIP models. '90–98% of baseline accuracy' therefore does not demonstrate competitiveness with the state of the art, and the two-stage distillation recipe makes the GS models strictly dependent on this already-limited teacher.

The headline accuracy gains are modest and potentially fragile: GS variants trail the RGB baseline on many datasets (e.g., fer2013 drops from 17.41 to 3.46–8.99, imagenet_sketch 10.27 to 2.69–8.87), with only relative-average metrics painted favorably. No repeated runs, seeds, or statistical significance are reported for the large-scale CLIP results.

The claimed systems contribution partially overlaps with prior engineering: the core kernels build directly on the open-source gsplat2d/GaussianImage/LIG codebase, and the speedup (up to 90×) is largely attributable to batch-parallelization (Amdahl's law scaling in Table 3 shows diminishing returns), which is a solid but incremental engineering effort rather than a fundamental advance.

Several important details are deferred or unclear: the pruning pipeline (a headline algorithmic contribution) is evaluated only on reconstruction quality on 100 Mini-ImageNet samples and never integrated into the CLIP training experiments; Appendix C for CUDA details is referenced but its content in the appendix is thin on implementation specifics; code is only promised, not released ('will soon be open-sourced').

The 'first large-scale exploration' framing somewhat overstates novelty relative to closely related concurrent work (GViT, GaussianToken) which the paper acknowledges but positions as 'small-scale' without a direct quantitative comparison.
